what: Two holdout-B files were read before the confirmation run, and no saved script accounts for it.
evidence: On this filesystem a file's access time changes only on the first read after it is written. I checked this: a probe file read at +3 s and again at +6 s kept the +3 s access time. The first reads of the B files were: cache/holdout_B/emg_contents_B.parquet at 12:22:15, emg_buildings_B.parquet at 14:15:21 and emg_motor_B.parquet at 14:27:15. confirm.py loads all three B files together, and confirm_round1.json was written at 14:28, so only the motor read matches confirm.py. The contents read happened during round-1 exploration and the buildings read just before it ended. A grep of the a31 tree and the whole scratchpad finds holdout_B only in build_cache.py, confirm.py, confirm_r2.py, r2_c0_inputs.py, the review folders and workflow_result.json. Every agent report says holdout_B was not opened. The reader cannot be identified from the files.
fix: Treat B as possibly seen. Any peek could only have helped a variation, and none passed, so the null result stands. Before any future adoption, keep the confirmation half outside the folders the agents can read, and record its hash and access time before and after exploration.

what: B2024 is not independent of evidence used to design the variations.
evidence: A30's E1 (A/E by factor, all 2024 rows), E2 and E5 (filled against as-is, scored on all 2024 rows) used B outcomes. The d4 data audit read the raw emerging claims.parquet, which holds every 2024 claim, for large-claim counts and development factors. Round 2 was built from these audits, and R1 is a variant of E5, so its B result was partly foreseeable.
fix: Note in the record that B tests the frozen configurations only, not the choice of ideas. Any bias runs towards the variations, so it cannot hide a gain.

what: confirm_r2.json is not valid JSON.
evidence: json.load fails with JSONDecodeError. Its first six lines are R3's stdout ('  buildings: power 0.931' and so on), printed before the array. confirm_round1.json parses.
fix: Send the progress prints from r3_slope.predict to stderr, or write the JSON with json.dump to a file.

what: The ratio r2.log prints for R4 (buildings c0_csy 1.0377) is an artefact, and R4 changes no new-business prediction at all.
evidence: c0_csy exists only on the 2025 rows, but the ratio divides its mean by C0's mean over the 2024 and 2025 rows together. Recomputed on the 2025 rows: new business ratio 1.0000, with 0 of 39,716 rows changed; renewals 0.9996, with 7.1% of 12,579 rows changed. On the developed backtest the new-business ratio is also exactly 1.0. The tree model puts 2024 and 2025 (and 2023 and 2024) on the same side of every split, so R4 is a no-op on the rows it was meant for. 'No effect on the backtest' is built in, not a finding.
fix: Record R4 as void (a no-op for new business), not as tested and rejected. Compute these ratios on the rows where the column exists.

what: The halves are badly matched for contents. This is chance, not a bug, but it distorts single-half reads.
evidence: Pooled C0 level-matched D2 is 0.12012 on A and 0.11981 on B. Contents is 0.09718 on A, the 96.75th percentile of 400 random customer halves, and 0.03103 on B, the 3.75th (random-half mean 0.06485, sd 0.01915). R3 sits at the 96.25th percentile on A and the 3.25th on B, which explains its +0.0008 / -0.0033 flip. On all of 2024 R3 is -0.00113 [95% -0.00321, +0.00115].
fix: Report the gain on all of 2024 next to B for variants with no parameter chosen on A, and read single-half signs with this spread in mind.

what: Round 2 was confirmed on half the available evidence, and the Holm families include members that can never be adopted.
evidence: R1, R2 and R3 had no parameter chosen on A, yet only B counted. Pooling A and B does not change any verdict: R2 +0.000256 [95% -0.000047, +0.000661], one-sided p 0.063; R1 -0.00019 (p 0.62); R1+R2 +0.00012 (p 0.22); R3 -0.00113 (p 0.85). In round 1, m = 9 includes v7, which returns C0 exactly (gain 0 on both halves), and v1, the owner decision that is never adopted. Both make the thresholds stricter, but the smallest p was 0.517 against a first threshold of 0.00278.
fix: For variants preregistered with no A tuning, confirm on all of 2024. Leave null and owner-only arms out of m, or report them separately.

what: The '+3.8% on the 2025 buildings mean' from R4 is a reporting artefact in r2_c0_inputs.py. The print line computes out[c].mean() / out.c0.mean() over the whole output frame. c0_csy exists only on the 2025 rows (NaN on the 14,867 rows from 2024, which mean() skips), while c0 is averaged over the 2024 and 2025 rows together. So 2025-only predictions are divided by a mean that includes the cheaper 2024 rows.
evidence: From r2_buildings.parquet, on the 2025 rows only: mean(c0_csy) / mean(c0) = 0.99992. The script printed 1.0377. Mean C0 is 455.28 on test2025 and 379.16 on A2024, which explains the gap. A fresh rebuild of the C0 models gives the same result: 0 of 39,716 new-business rows change, 7.1% of 12,579 renewals change, and the 2025 mean ratio is 0.99992. The c0_csy column itself is correct; only the printed summary is wrong.
fix: Compute each ratio over the rows where the column is defined, per split. For example: m = out[c].notna(); out.loc[m, c].mean() / out.loc[m, 'c0'].mean(), grouped by split. Correct the narrative too: R4 is not a level lever (it moves the 2025 buildings mean by -0.008%).

what: R3 fits the power to C0 itself (log mu = a + b log c0). C0 is rate times exposure, so b also changes the exposure elasticity: predictions become proportional to e^b instead of e. This matters because the share of part-year rows doubles between the fitting year and the scored year. The code matches PREREGISTERED_RULE.md literally, so the defect is in the rule's specification.
evidence: Share of rows with exposure under 0.5: 2023 fit rows 9.7% / 11.0% / 13.2%; A2024 18.8% / 20.5% / 21.8% (buildings / contents / motor). Nelder-Mead converged: its b values agree with an exact profile fit to 1e-8 (0.931 / 1.142 / 0.842). Fitting the power to the rate instead, with exposure kept proportional (mu = e * exp(a) * (c0/e)^b), gives b = 0.907 / 1.086 / 0.882. Level-matched pooled gain for that version: A -0.00018 (p 0.546), B -0.00182 (p 0.922). As run: A +0.00078, B -0.00331. Both versions fail.
fix: In any future calibration-power variant, apply the power to the rate (c0 / exposure) and multiply by exposure afterwards, and write the rule that way before running it.

what: R1's imputation is a field-by-field draw from the region's distribution of each field. It ignores two better sources of information. First, smoke_alarms is a policy-level field whose value is known at the same address in an earlier year for most gaps. Second, it ignores how fields relate to observed covariates (for example soil type to the address's location fields). Rebuilding x_clay_dry from the drawn soil type is correct, but it is what makes R1 hurt buildings: imputed 'clay' switches on the dry-summer term at random.
evidence: For smoke_alarms, 71.9% of 2024 gap rows and 22.2% of 2025 gap rows have a known earlier-year value at the same address. Where an address has both 2023 and 2024 values (9,388 addresses), they agree 100% of the time. The other buildings fields are missing for the whole address, so nothing can be carried forward. Same random draws with and without the x_clay_dry rebuild: buildings per-line gain on A is -0.00302 with the rebuild and -0.00202 without; on B, -0.00064 with and +0.00031 without. Pooled gain on B without the rebuild is +0.00061 (p 0.116), which still fails Holm (the loosest threshold is 0.025). Changing the seed (all lines, seed 100) moves the pooled gain to -0.00076 on A and +0.00038 on B, so Monte Carlo noise is about 0.0002 at most.
fix: Carry forward the address's earlier-year smoke_alarms before drawing at random, and draw soil type conditional on the address's own location fields rather than the region alone. Holdout B has already been used to confirm round 2, so any such variant needs a new holdout.

what: R4 cannot work for this model, so the backtest cannot test it. The buildings XGBoost splits on customer_since_year only at old values. Every value from 2020 onwards (from 2021 in the backtest model) falls on the same side of every split, so shifting new business (2025 to 2024; 2024 to 2023 in the backtest) or recent renewals changes nothing. Structurally, the backtest is the right analogue: in both cases the new business's customer_since_year is one above the highest value in the fitting years. But there is no effect for it to find, and the backtest model's split points differ from the final model's.
evidence: Final model: 5 split nodes on customer_since_year, at 2008 / 2011 / 2015 / 2020, carrying 0.11% of total split gain. Backtest model: 14 nodes, at 2011 to 2021, 0.38% of gain. Rows that change: new business 0% in both; backtest renewals 10.5% (all with customer_since_year of 2021 or earlier); 2025 renewals 7.1%. Backtest re-run: gain -2.09e-06, 95% CI [-7.3e-05, +5.5e-05]. The fresh rebuild reproduces this exactly.
fix: Record R4 as inert by construction rather than 'tested, no effect'. Before testing a fix to an out-of-range field, check whether the model splits anywhere near the range in question.

what: The R2 premise that emerging vehicles are 'shifted by two years' is only approximate, and the floor at 0 never applies. The shift reaches only the small-claim GLM, which is correct: the motor large-claim GLM does not use vehicle_age.
evidence: Emerging minus developed (2021-24 pooled) at the 5 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 90 / 95th percentiles: 3 / 2 / 3 / 3 / 2 / 3 years. Mean gap: 2.52 pooled; 1.88 against developed 2024 alone (10.67 vs 8.79). The emerging minimum is 3, so 0 rows hit the floor. The shift changes the small-claim GLM's prediction on 88.1% of 2024 rows (the 11.9% missing vehicle_age stay as they were) and the large-claim GLM on 0%. Vehicle_age spline knots on the developed data: 0 / 5 / 9 / 28.
fix: None needed for the code. A different shift (for example 3) has not been tested, and testing it now would be post hoc; it needs a new holdout.

what: Outside round 2, found while checking C0's inputs: C0 predicts emerging contents rows with plain exposure, although the developed contents GLM was fitted with seasonal exposure (rule D-22). Emerging.Context never calls use_window on the emerging lines.
evidence: On emerging contents rows, exposure equals exposure_plain exactly in every split. On developed contents rows, 26% differ by more than 1% (ratio 0.943 to 1.127). I recovered the final-window month weights exactly from the developed rows (maximum relative error 3e-12) and applied them to the emerging rows. Pooled level-matched gain: fit2023 -0.00002; A2024 -0.00020 (CI [-0.00030, -0.00010]; contents line -0.00110). So the inconsistency is real, but correcting it makes the score worse.
fix: Leave C0 as it is. Add a line to A31's notes that this was checked and rejected.

what: The x0.91 / +0.003 reading of the leaderboard rests on a one-common-scale assumption that our own data falsify. The audit said nothing was left to test it. In fact the three scores and the emerging claims data test it, and it fails.
evidence: The exact fit (s1_common_scale.py) reproduces the audit: k 0.912 (0.9118-0.9121 across the 5 dp rounding box), gain +0.0034 (0.00337-0.00341), best score 0.1594. To fit, it has to imply C/N = 8*sum(sqrt y)/null deviance = 2.35 and 4*sum(sqrt(level-matched mu))/N = 1.60. Emerging 2023, 2024 A and 2024 B give C/N 0.25-0.27 and 0.55-0.58 under three readings of the metric (s2_calib2024.py). The 2024 bootstrap 95% ranges are 0.245-0.269 and 0.557-0.581. C/N stays at 0.244 reweighted to the 2025 line by new-business mix and rises only to 0.368 at double the claim frequency (s4_checks.py). Holding C/N in 0.22-0.37, no common scale fits the three scores: residuals are about (+0.0003, -0.0012, +0.0009), 230 times the rounding (s1b_common_rejected.py). The method was also run on the 2024 halves, where the truth is known (s9_validate.py). It returned C/N of 2.01, 2.28, -0.17 and -0.17 against a truth of 0.25-0.27. In the case most like 2025 (A2024, as-is x0.8) it predicted +0.0041 at x0.903 when the true best common scale was x0.966, worth +0.00017.
fix: Withdraw 'x0.91, worth about +0.003 (score about 0.159)' from MODEL_DOCUMENTATION 11.4 item 4 and from the A30 leaderboard entry in AUDIT_LOG. Replace it with the family result: the best common scale is 0.92-1.05 of as-is, worth at most +0.0009 (+0.0018 in a wider box). A x0.912 file is predicted to score 0.1536-0.1569 (median 0.1550), below as-is in 74-83% of sampled solutions.

what: 'Per-line levels cannot be separated from three files' is too pessimistic, and it hides the one robust signal the board gives: motor new business. Once C/N is held in its data-consistent range, the NB-scenario file pins the motor new-business scale near the as-is level.
evidence: All three files are exact rescales of as-is: level reset by line, the NB scenario by line and new business (ratios constant within segment to 1e-9). The p = 1.5 identity is exact; s4 check error is 4e-16. Over all solutions with C/N 0.22-0.37 and scales in [0.7, 1.4] (s5c_ranges.py), motor new business sits at 0.99-1.18 and motor renewals at 0.70-0.95. Motor NB/renewal is 1.09-1.66, with NB above renewals in 100% of solutions. This is unchanged under +-1.5% public-weight error and the rounding (s5e). The level reset's motor x0.768 is 15-35% too low for motor new business. Contents runs the other way: the line sits at 0.70-0.93, and contents NB is above renewals in only 28% of solutions. Buildings is not identified.
fix: Reopen D-37 with this as leaderboard evidence. Any loading should be motor-specific (and possibly buildings), not contents. Report the 2025 level shift as concentrated in motor new business, not as a uniform 15-20%.

what: The quadratic in log total ratio is presented beside the exact fit as if it agreed. Its own gain is a third of the claimed +0.003, and it treats segment-wise rescales as common rescales.
evidence: s1_common_scale.py: the quadratic in log total ratio gives an optimum of x0.9427 and a gain of +0.00098. The exact deviance model applied to totals gives x0.9427 and +0.00097. The two methods the audit cites therefore disagree on the gain by a factor of 3.5, and neither survives the C/N check.
fix: Drop both. State that the files differ by line and new business, so no scalar-level model of the three scores is valid.

what: 'On this reading the level explains at most a fifth of the gap' rests on the falsified model. The three scores bound the level gain from below, not from above.
evidence: s5_family.py, s5d_plausible.py and s5f_line_gain.py, C/N 0.22-0.37. The public gain from line by new-business scales is 0.0024-0.0087 with scales in [0.7, 1.4] (median of sampled solutions 0.0045), 14-51% of the 0.017 gap. It is 0.0024-0.0171 in [0.6, 1.5], 0.0024-0.0139 in [0.6, 1.5] with NB/renewal 1.0-1.6, and up to 0.027-0.029 in [0.5, 1.6]. Per-line scales alone give 0.0002-0.0066 in [0.7, 1.4].
fix: Replace it with: level (line by new business) is worth at least about 0.0024 on the public board, plausibly up to about 0.009, and the three scores cannot cap it further. Only probes can settle it.

what: Gains read off the public board overstate what reaches the private board, which decides the result. Neither the audit nor any probing plan allows for this.
evidence: s6_noise.py and s8_level_noise.py, 2024 customer bootstrap scaled to 2025 row counts. The public-against-private relative SE of the optimal scale per segment is 7-31% (buildings renewals 28-31%, motor new business 7%). Expected private loss from using public scales is 0.0021-0.0025 for six scales and 0.0012-0.0014 for three. In-sample optimism on the public board is +0.0010-0.0017 for six scales. A public gain of about 0.003 at line by new-business level is therefore worth about zero on the private board unless it is shrunk.
fix: Credibility-weight public-identified scales with the 2023-24 estimates before adopting them. Select the final submission explicitly: under rule 2.b, the best public score is auto-selected otherwise.

what: Any per-line reading of the NB-scenario score is invalid. This analysis's own first pass made that error; it is recorded here so nobody repeats it.
evidence: s4_checks.py: on 2024 rows with known truth, the per-line solver fed the NB-scenario file returned (0.62, 0.08, 1.01) for true per-line scales of (0.68, 0.73, 0.77). The per-line design has condition number 189. The intermediate s3_perline.py, which claimed a minimum gain of 0.0126, is superseded.
fix: Use the NB-scenario score only in the six-segment (line by new business) model.

what: The 2025 public board is structurally unlike the 2024 holdout that A31 rounds 1-2 tested ranking on, so 'nothing passes on 2024' may not carry over to 2025.
evidence: s6_noise.py: C0's line by new-business level-matched pooled D2 is 0.118 on 2024 (A 0.121, B 0.120). On the 2025 public board the as-is file scores 0.156 raw and at least 0.158 level-matched. The SD of the pooled score at public size is 0.0078-0.0101, so the gap is about 4-5 SD.
fix: Note it in A31. Ranking conclusions drawn on 2024 rows (9% new business) need a caveat for a 77% new-business 2025 book.

what: A30's reading of the leaderboard (one common scale for every row, best at x0.91 of as is, worth about +0.003) cannot be true under the stated metric. A30 says the fit is 'exactly identified, with nothing left to test the assumption'. That is wrong: the assumption fixes how sensitive the score is to rescaling (4 sum sqrt(asis) / N), and outcomes of this kind cannot produce the sensitivity the fit needs.
evidence: check8_bound.py: at s 0.91 the observed as-is minus level-reset drop (+0.00580) needs 4 sum W / N = 1.791. N >= 8 sum sqrt(mu)(1 - R) holds row by row for any baseline. R = sum sqrt(y) / sum sqrt(mu) measures 0.231 (2023) and 0.226 (2024), which caps the ratio at 0.749 even at R = 0.3. check9_realised_bound.py: for any realised outcome, with only 80% of rows claim-free (the actual share in 2023-24 is 92.6%), the cap is 1.188 (rate null) or 1.168 (mean null). check3_null_backtest.py: the same null extrapolation reproduces the 2024 pooled D2 (0.1147 predicted against 0.1179 actual; claim-size term actual / predicted 0.98-1.01). At s 0.91 that null predicts drops of +0.00206 and +0.00046 against the observed +0.00580 and +0.00150.
fix: Withdraw the x0.91 recommendation and the claim that the level explains at most a fifth of the gap to the leader. Re-read the board with N set by the claim-size distribution (check12) and identify each line's level with probe pairs (check14).

what: A31 level-matches every line on the scored rows, so it cannot see the largest lever: line and new-business level structure on the 2025 book. Its null result does not support 'the rest is risk ranking or noise'.
evidence: Using only the two score differences, with N between 0.8 and 1.25 times the estimate, both null definitions and buildings from 0.6 to 1.4 (check12_robust_lines.py, 30 of 30 fits exact): contents comes out at 0.28-0.68 of as is and motor at 0.97-1.28. Per-line optimal levels gain +0.0054 to +0.0301 over as is; the x0.91 file gains -0.0030 to +0.0026. The ranking gains on A31's harness are of order 0.002 at most (check6, check10).
fix: Treat line and new-business levels as the main open question, settled on the board by single-line probe pairs, and stop ranking searches on the level-matched harness for this purpose.

what: The pre-registered rule adopts a combination only if every part passes pooled, so a variation that helps one line on both halves can never be adopted. V3's motor component is such a case.
evidence: check6_ensemble.py: V3 motor as frozen, pooled gain +0.00142 on A and +0.00277 on B. Every blend weight (0.25 to 1.0) and every seed (3103, 7, 2031) is positive on both halves. check10_v3_motor.py, three-seed geometric mean, 50/50 with C0: A +0.00112 [-0.00057, +0.00311], B +0.00241 [+0.00025, +0.00532], A+B +0.00175 [+0.00027, +0.00362], share not better 0.010. This is post hoc: motor was picked after both halves were seen.
fix: If wanted, pre-register a per-line rule. Treat the V3 motor blend as a labelled post-hoc option worth about +0.002, below the 0.003 bar.

what: confirm_r2.json is not valid JSON. Progress lines ('buildings: power 0.931' and so on) are printed before the array, so json.load fails on it.
evidence: json.decoder.JSONDecodeError at line 1, column 3 when check6_ensemble.py loaded it. I parsed it from the first newline-bracket instead.
fix: Write the JSON to the file and send the progress lines to stderr, or strip them.
